1.pericope_label: The sons of God take wives of the daughters of men

schools.summary: Lay out the interpretative options before choosing, since everything in the chapter depends on this verse. Three views of the sons of the Elohim have been entertained from the very earliest times: that they were the sons of princes, that they were angels, or that they were the Sethites; and correspondingly the daughters of men have been taken for the daughters of people of the lower orders, of mankind generally, or of the Cainites. State also the plain sense of the increase: the verse relates to the multiplication of men generally, without any restriction, that is, of the whole human race. Then argue the case rather than assert it. Against the Sethite view, which is the one most generally accepted in modern times, press a question nobody has answered: how could such marriages produce mighty men, men of renown, or how could strong warriors be the result of pious men intermarrying with women of an inferior race? Note that the Jewish interpreters, who well understood the uses of their own language, are right in the main point, that the phrase sons of the Elohim conveys no idea of moral goodness or piety; Elohim constantly means mighty ones, and is elsewhere translated judges, while in Job the sons of Elohim are the nobles gathered round a king at his durbar. Then apply the ordinary rule of interpretation: the daughters of the adam in the first verse must be the same as the daughters of the adam in the second, and the adam here spoken of are the Sethites, since the phrase occurs in the history of Noah just after his descent from Adam and Cain is passed over altogether. On the increase itself, allow that it must have been comparatively slow, because of the great age each patriarch attained before his first-born, and remember that the name given is not necessarily the eldest son but the one who enjoyed the birthright, Noah, born when his father was a hundred and eighty-two, being a case in point. Yet Cain built a city, so a considerable population settling round him was at least possible; and it was probably about the time of Enoch that the corruption of the family of Adam began to be general.

Set the scene before the sin: the world was then as if divided into two parts, because the family of Seth cherished the pure and lawful worship of God, from which the rest had fallen. Although all mankind had been formed for the worship of God, and sincere religion ought everywhere to have reigned, yet since the greater part had prostituted itself either to contempt of God or to depraved superstitions, it was fitting that the small portion God had adopted by special privilege should remain separate. It was therefore base ingratitude in the posterity of Seth to mingle themselves with the children of Cain and with other profane races, since they voluntarily deprived themselves of the inestimable grace of God; it was an intolerable profanation to pervert and confound the order appointed by God. Answer the objection that this seems a light matter. It is no light crime to violate a distinction established by the Lord; the separation of the worshippers of God from profane nations was a sacred appointment which ought reverently to have been observed, in order that a Church of God might exist upon earth; and the disease was desperate, seeing that men rejected the remedy divinely prescribed for them. Dispose of the rival readings briefly and without ceremony. The ancient figment concerning the intercourse of angels with women is abundantly refuted by its own absurdity, and it is surprising that learned men should formerly have been fascinated by ravings so gross and prodigious; while the opinion of the Chaldean paraphrase, that promiscuous marriages between the sons of nobles and the daughters of plebeians are condemned, is merely frigid. Moses does not distinguish the sons of God from the daughters of men because they were of dissimilar nature or different origin, but because they were the sons of God by adoption, whom he had set apart for himself, while the rest remained in their original condition. Then say precisely what is condemned in the marriages, and what is not. It is not that regard was had to beauty in the choice of a wife, nor is fornication the charge here, but that mere lust reigned; for marriage is a thing too sacred to allow that men should be induced to it by the lust of the eyes, this union being inseparable and comprising all the parts of life. That they took wives of all that they chose signifies that they did not make their choice from those possessed of the necessary endowments, but wandered without discrimination, rushing onward according to their lust. And add the consequence, which is the point of the whole: it was impossible but that the sons of God should degenerate when they thus bound themselves in the same yoke with unbelievers.

Begin by fixing the chronology, since the English is misleading: it was not at this time that men began to multiply, but the inspired penman speaks now of a fact which had taken place long before. Then identify the parties from the distinction the verse itself draws between men and those called the sons of God, and take the latter for the children of God among whom the true religion was at first preserved, and the former for the irreligious. Say what the marriages were: those who were called by the name of the Lord, and called upon that name, married the daughters of men, that is, those that were profane and strangers to God; the posterity of Seth did not keep to themselves as they ought, but intermingled with the race of Cain. Then name the fault exactly, and let the text supply it: they took them wives of all that they chose, so they chose only by the eye, since they saw that they were fair, which was all they looked at. Draw the wider lesson from the blessing turned curse. Men began to multiply upon the face of the earth: this was the effect of the blessing given at the creation, and yet man's corruption so abused this blessing that it turned into a curse. That is worth pressing, because it is the pattern of the whole chapter, in which every gift of God becomes an occasion of sin to a race that will not be governed. Keep the treatment brief here, since the substance of the corruption is described more fully in the verses that follow, and reserve the detail for them; but do not let the brevity soften the verdict, for what is described is a general apostasy of the professing part of mankind, not a lapse of a few.

Explain first why so full an account of the world's degeneracy is given before the history of its ruin: it is for the glory of God's justice, and for warning to a wicked world, that the destroying of it may be seen to be an act not of absolute sovereignty but of necessary justice, for the maintaining of the honour of God's government. Then give the two occasions of the wickedness in order. The first is the increase of mankind. This was the effect of the blessing, and yet man's corruption so abused and perverted the blessing that it was turned into a curse; thus sin takes occasion by the mercies of God to be the more exceedingly sinful. When the wicked are multiplied, transgression increaseth: the more sinners the more sin, and the multitude of offenders emboldens men. Infectious diseases are most destructive in populous cities, and sin is a spreading leprosy; even in the New Testament church, when the number of the disciples was multiplied, there arose a murmuring. Numerous families need to be well governed, lest they become wicked families. The second occasion is mixed marriages. The sons of God, that is, the professors of religion who were called by the name of the Lord and called upon that name, married the daughters of men, that is, those that were profane and strangers to God and godliness; the posterity of Seth did not keep by themselves, as they ought to have done, both for the preservation of their own purity and in detestation of the apostasy, but intermingled themselves with the excommunicated race of Cain. Then ask what was amiss in these marriages, and answer in three parts. They chose only by the eye, for they saw that they were fair, which was all they looked at. They followed the choice which their own corrupt affections made, taking all that they chose, without advice and consideration. And, what proved of such bad consequence, they married strange wives and were unequally yoked with unbelievers, a thing afterwards forbidden to Israel, which was the unhappy occasion of Solomon's apostasy and was of bad consequence to the Jews after their return out of Babylon. Draw the rule for the reader's own household: professors of religion, in marrying both themselves and their children, should make conscience of keeping within the bounds of profession, for the bad will sooner debauch the good than the good reform the bad; and those that profess themselves the children of God must not marry without his consent, which they have not if they join in affinity with his enemies.

debates.question: Whose multiplying is meant, and when?

sides.position: The whole human race
The posterity of Cain, mere natural men, multiplying faster than Seth's line because polygamy had spread after Lamech's example
Growth must have been slow, each patriarch reaching a great age before the son who is named, though Cain's city shows a considerable population was already possible
The multiplying is not to be dated here at all, the writer speaking of what had happened long before
The increase itself was the first cause of the wickedness, the blessing so abused that it turned into a curse

debates.question: Who were the sons of God?

sides.position: Three answers have been held from the earliest times — the sons of princes, angels, or the Sethites — with the daughters of men correspondingly of the lower orders, of mankind at large, or of the Cainites
The Sethites, by elimination: angels are incorporeal and neither marry nor generate, and marrying beneath oneself is no crime and could produce at most a partial corruption
The Sethites: the figment of intercourse between angels and women is refuted by its own absurdity, and the Chaldee reading of nobles and plebeians is merely frigid
The reverse of the accepted view: the phrase conveys no idea of piety but constantly means mighty ones, so the pious are the women and the mighty are the intruders

debates.question: What was wrong with the marriages?

sides.position: Three faults — they chose only by the eye, they followed their own corrupt affections without advice, and they were unequally yoked with unbelievers
Neither the regard to beauty nor fornication is charged, but that mere lust reigned; and graver still, the confounding of the sacred separation of God's worshippers from profane nations

outliers.note: Alone turns the accepted reading round, asking how the marriage of pious men to women of an inferior race could produce mighty men and men of renown, and making the women the pious party and the mighty the intruders.

Alone makes the multiplying itself the engine of the corruption, noting that the more sinners the more sin and that a multitude of offenders emboldens men, as infectious diseases are deadliest in populous cities and sin is a spreading leprosy.

themes: when men began to multiply on the face of the earth
the sons of God saw the daughters of men that they were fair
they took them wives of all which they chose

3.pericope_label: My spirit shall not always strive with man; the giants in the earth

schools.summary: Settle the disputed verb by the purpose of the verse rather than by the lexicon alone. The verb signifies to rule, to preside over, to sit as judge, and only by consequence to strive; the versions generally take it as shall not dwell or abide. But the main purpose and context of the verse is the divine determination to shorten human life, and that fixes the meaning whichever way one takes the spirit: whether it is the animating breath by which human life is sustained, or the spiritual part of man, his conscience and moral sense, in opposition to his flesh, the struggle henceforward is not to be indefinitely prolonged. Read the sentence literally, then, as saying that the divine gift of life shall not rule in man for ever, that is, for a period so protracted as antediluvian life; and take the hundred and twenty years accordingly as the reduced span, that which under the most favourable sanitary influences might still be its normal length, and not as a countdown to the deluge. Understand the spirit itself as the divine spirit of life bestowed on man, the principle of physical and ethical, natural and spiritual life, which God will now withdraw, thereby putting an end to their life and conduct. On the giants, resist the English word. Nephilim comes from a root meaning to fall upon, and signifies the invaders; Luther gives the correct sense, tyrants, so called because they fell upon the people and oppressed them, and he rejected the notion that they were giants, to which the Greek rendering gave rise, as fabulous. Yet allow the other possibility its due: nothing is more probable than that at a time when men lived for centuries human vigour should show itself in producing a race of more than ordinary height, and the Nephilim appear elsewhere as a race of great physical strength and stature. They were apparently of the Cainite stock, and the text carefully distinguishes them from the offspring of the mixed marriages. Note finally that gibborim, the mighty men, has nothing to do with stature but means heroes or warriors, and is generally used in a good sense; the children of these marriages were a race of brave fighting men who by their martial deeds won themselves reputation.

Explain why God is introduced as speaking in his own person: there is greater weight in a declaration pronounced by God's own mouth, that the wickedness of men was too deplorable to leave any hope of remedy. This was necessary because at the bare hearing of so terrible an example of divine anger we are even now afraid, and men commonly do not refrain from accusing God of excessive haste, or even deem him cruel for taking vengeance; so Moses pronounces, in the person of God, that the depravity of the world was intolerable and obstinately incurable by any remedy. On the disputed word, canvass the derivations and reject the worst. Some of the Hebrews derive it from a root meaning a scabbard, and elicit the sense that God was unwilling for his Spirit to be any longer held captive in a human body, as a sword is enclosed in its sheath; but that exposition is distorted and savours of the delirium of the Manichees, as if the soul of man were a portion of the Divine Spirit, and it is to be rejected. The more commonly received Jewish opinion derives it from another root, but since that root means sometimes one thing and sometimes another, different interpretations arise from it, and the matter is not to be settled hastily. On the giants, do not suppose that all the men of the age are meant, but certain individuals who, being stronger than the rest and relying on their own might and power, exalted themselves unlawfully and without measure. The grammarians do not agree about the etymology: some think they were so called because they exceeded the common stature, others because the countenance of men fell at the sight of them on account of the enormous size of their body, others because all fell prostrate through terror of their magnitude. There seems more truth in the opinion that a similitude is taken from a torrent or an impetuous tempest, for as a storm violently falling lays waste and destroys the fields, so these robbers brought destruction and desolation into the world. Insist on the point that decides it: Moses does not say that they were of extraordinary stature, but only that they were robust, and he distinguishes them from other men not so much by the size of their bodies as by their robberies and their lust of dominion. Note also that Jerome rendered the passage in the worst possible manner, making the giants the offspring of the intercourse described in the next clause, where the Greek rightly has and after this.

Take the striving as the Spirit's work upon the conscience, and say by what means it was carried on: the Spirit strove by Noah's preaching and by inward checks, but it was in vain with the most of men. It is only by the influence of the Spirit of God that the carnal mind can be subdued and destroyed, and those who wilfully resist and grieve that Spirit must ultimately be left to the hardness and blindness of their own hearts if they do not repent and turn to God. Give the reason the text gives, for that he also is flesh: incurably corrupt and sensual, so that it is labour lost to strive with him; and press the also, that is, all, one as well as another, for they are all sunk into the mire of flesh. Then take the hundred and twenty years as a reprieve, not a lifespan. Even at this time the earth was ripe for destruction, but God promised them a hundred and twenty years' respite: if they repented in that interim, well; if not, they should be destroyed by a flood. So long will God defer the judgment they deserve, and give them space to prevent it by their repentance and reformation; justice said, cut them down, but mercy interceded, Lord, let them alone this year also, and so far mercy prevailed that a reprieve was obtained for six score years. God delights in mercy, and therefore a gracious warning is given. On the giants, derive Nephilim from a root meaning he fell, and take them for those who had apostatised or fallen from the true religion; complain that the Greek translated the word by one which literally signifies earth-born, which we follow in saying giants, without reference to the meaning, generally conceiving it to signify persons of enormous stature. Properly understood, the word makes a very just distinction between the sons of men and the sons of God: those were the fallen earth-born men, with the animal and devilish mind; these were born from above. Note that gibborim signifies properly conquerors or heroes, from a root meaning he prevailed, and that men of the name means twice named, having one name derived from their fathers and another acquired by their daring exploits; and observe that our translators have rendered seven different Hebrew words by the one term giants, by which are probably meant persons of great knowledge, piety, courage or wickedness, and not men of enormous stature.

Read the threatening as a token of God's displeasure at those who married strange wives: he threatens to withdraw from them his Spirit, whom they had grieved by such marriages, contrary to their convictions; fleshly lusts are often punished with spiritual judgments, the sorest of all judgments. Or take it as another occasion of the great wickedness of the old world, the Spirit of the Lord, being provoked by their resistance of his motions, ceasing to strive with them, so that all religion was soon lost among them; and note that God warns them of this beforehand, that they might not further vex his Holy Spirit but by their prayers might stay him with them. Then observe two things in the verse. First, God's resolution not always to strive with man by his Spirit. The blessed Spirit strives with sinners, by the convictions and admonitions of conscience, to turn them from sin to God; if the Spirit be resisted, quenched, and striven against, though he strive long, he will not strive always; and those are ripening apace for ruin whom the Spirit of grace has left off striving with. Second, the reason of that resolution, that he also is flesh, incurably corrupt and carnal and sensual, so that it is labour lost to strive with him: can the Ethiopian change his skin? Then turn to the giants and describe the temptation they were under to oppress and do violence. They were too hard for all about them and carried all before them, with their great bulk, as the sons of Anak, and with their great name, as the king of Assyria; and thus armed they daringly insulted the rights of all their neighbours and trampled upon all that is just and sacred. Draw the moral from that, since it is the use of the passage: those that have so much power over others as to be able to oppress them have seldom so much power over themselves as not to oppress, and great might is a very great snare to many. Note finally the irony of their renown: this degenerate race slighted the honour their ancestors had obtained by virtue and religion, and made themselves a great name by that which was the perpetual ruin of their good name.

debates.question: What does the verb rendered strive mean?

sides.position: To rule, and to judge as the consequence of ruling; the spirit is the divine principle of life, now to be withdrawn
More exactly to rule or preside, though the versions generally render it dwell or abide; either way the context fixes the sense, that the struggle is not to be indefinitely prolonged
Reject the derivation that makes the word a scabbard, as though the Spirit were held captive in the body like a sword in its sheath — a distorted reading redolent of Manichean delirium
The Spirit's ordinary work upon conscience, by Noah's preaching and by inward checks, which where resisted and quenched will not always continue

debates.question: What are the hundred and twenty years?

sides.position: A reprieve before the flood, justice saying cut them down and mercy interceding to let them alone this year also
A divine determination to shorten human life, reducing its extreme duration to what might still be its normal length; the number is a lifespan, not a countdown
The same, since the withdrawal of the divine principle of life is what ends the long lives
Those fallen from the true religion, the Greek rendering having given us giants without regard to the sense
Tyrants, so called because they fell upon the people and oppressed them, Luther rejecting the giant sense as fabulous
Robbers who laid waste the world as a storm falling violently lays waste the fields; Moses calls them robust, not tall
Actual stature: an age of long lives is likely to have produced a taller race

outliers.note: Alone defends the literal stature of the Nephilim, thinking an age of long lives likely to have produced a taller race, and citing Lenormant for a root meaning to be wonderful, compared with an Assyrian word for an ogre unique in size.
Alone observes that the saying was spoken by God within himself rather than to Noah, who has not yet been mentioned in the narrative.

themes: My spirit shall not always strive with man, for that he also is flesh
yet his days shall be an hundred and twenty years
There were giants in the earth in those days

5.pericope_label: The wickedness of man; it repented the Lord; but Noah found grace

schools.summary: Render the sentence precisely before drawing anything from it: every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil the whole day, that is, continually and altogether evil. Gloss the word rendered imagination as form or shape, so that what is meant is every idea or embodied thought which presented itself to the mind through the working of the heart, that is, of the whole inner nature of man; and press the temporal phrase, all the day, from morning to night, without reproof of conscience or fear of the Divine justice. A more forcible picture of complete depravity could scarcely be drawn, and this corruption of man's inner nature is to be ascribed to the overthrow of moral and social restraints. Then use the verse as evidence in the question left open earlier, for the determination and the motive assigned here are irreconcilable with the angel-theory: had the godless race which God destroyed by the flood sprung either wholly or in part from the marriage of angels with the daughters of men, it would no longer have been the race first created by God in Adam, but a grotesque product of the Adamitic factor and an entirely foreign angelic one. On the repentance ascribed to God, do not resolve it by a figure but by an antinomy. If we begin with the omniscience and omnipotence of God as our postulates, everything upon earth must be predestined and immutably foreordained; if we start with man's free will, everything will depend upon human choice and action; both these sides must be true, though our mental powers are too limited to combine them. In Holy Scripture the latter view is kept the more prominently in the foreground, because upon it depends human responsibility; and so here the overwhelming of mankind by a flood, and the subsequent abbreviation of life, is set before our eyes as painful to the Deity and contrary to his goodwill towards men, but as necessitated by the extreme depravity of even the chosen race. On the sentence itself, render the verb delete or rub out, and limit its scope: the animal world was to share in the destruction because its fate is bound up with that of man, but the idea of the total destruction of all animals, so far from being contained in the text, is contradicted by it, since it says only that the destruction is to reach to them; wild beasts are not mentioned, probably because the domestic cattle would be the chief sufferers. Note last that this is the first place in the Bible where grace is mentioned, and that with these words the book of the generations of Adam ends: the purpose was not extermination but regeneration, and with Noah a higher and better order of things was to begin.

Show first that God was neither too harsh nor precipitate, since men commonly accuse him of haste and even deem him cruel. The word used indicates long continued patience: God had not proclaimed his sentence until, after well observing and long considering their case, he saw them past recovery. Then weigh the two clauses. That their wickedness was great in the earth carries its own emphasis, for he might have pardoned sins of a less aggravated character, and if impiety had reigned in one part only, other regions might have remained free from punishment; but now that iniquity has reached its highest point and so pervaded the whole earth that integrity possesses no longer a single corner, the time for punishment is more than fully arrived. Say it plainly: the earth was not overwhelmed with a deluge of waters till it had first been immersed in the pollution of wickedness. Then observe that Moses, having traced the cause of the deluge to external acts of iniquity, now ascends higher and declares that men were not only perverse by habit and by the custom of evil living, but that wickedness was too deeply seated in their hearts to leave any hope of repentance. On the repentance ascribed to God, be exact, for the passage is much abused. It does not properly belong to him, but has reference to our understanding of him; since we cannot comprehend him as he is, it is necessary that for our sakes he should in a certain sense transform himself. That repentance cannot take place in God appears from this single consideration, that nothing happens which is by him unexpected or unforeseen; and the same reasoning applies to the grief, for God is not sorrowful or sad, but remains for ever like himself in his celestial and happy repose. Yet because it could not otherwise be known how great is God's hatred and detestation of sin, the Spirit accommodates himself to our capacity. There is no need to involve ourselves in thorny questions when it is obvious to what end these words are applied: they teach that from the time man was so greatly corrupted, God would not reckon him among his creatures, as if he would say, this is not my workmanship, this is not that man who was formed in my image and whom I had adorned with such excellent gifts. On the beasts, meet the objection that it seems to exceed the bounds of moderation to be angry with unoffending animals: it is not wonderful that creatures made for man's sake, and living for his use, should participate in his ruin, for neither asses nor oxen had done evil, yet being in subjection to man when he fell they were drawn with him into the same destruction. And on Noah's finding grace, warn against the futile subtlety of those unlearned men who infer that if men find grace in God's sight it is because they seek it by their own industry and merits; for whence did Noah attain his integrity but from the preventing grace of God? The commencement of this favour was gratuitous mercy.

Draw the character of the antediluvian world in numbered strokes, since the indictment is cumulative. They were flesh, wholly sensual, the desires of the mind overwhelmed and lost in the desires of the flesh, their souls no longer discerning their high destiny but ever minding earthly things. They were in a state of wickedness, all corrupt within and unrighteous without, so that neither the science nor the practice of religion existed; piety was gone, and every form of sound words had disappeared. This wickedness was multiplied, continually increasing, so that the whole earth was corrupt before God and filled with violence, profligacy among the lower and cruelty and oppression among the higher classes being alike predominant. And all the imaginations of their thoughts were evil: the very first embryo of every idea, the figment of every thought, the very materials out of which perception and conception were formed, were all evil, the fountain which produced them incurably poisoned. Add what the sins were like in the doing: abundance of sin committed in all places by all sorts of people, sins in their own nature most gross and heinous, and committed daringly, with a defiance of heaven; and they did not do evil only through carelessness, but deliberately and designedly, contriving how to do mischief. Trace it to its root, which is the point of the verse: this was the bitter root and the corrupt spring, for all the violence and oppression, all the luxury and wantonness that was in the world proceeded from the corruption of nature. On the repentance, guard God's honour without softening the displeasure. The expressions are after the manner of men and must be so understood as not to reflect upon God's immutability or felicity; they do not speak any passion or uneasiness in God, for nothing can create disturbance to the eternal mind, but they speak his just and holy displeasure against sin and sinners. Neither do they speak any change of God's mind, for with him there is no variableness, but a change of his way: when God had made man upright he rested and was refreshed, and his way towards him showed him well pleased with the work of his own hands; but now that man was apostatised he could not do otherwise than show himself displeased, so that the change was in man, not in God. On the sentence, give the verb its force: I will wipe off man from off the earth, as dirt is wiped off from a place which should be clean; or I will blot out man, as lines are blotted out of a book which displease the author, or as the name of a citizen is blotted out of the rolls when he is disfranchised. And say why the beasts go with him: they were made for man, and therefore must be destroyed with man, since the end of their creation also was frustrated. Close on Noah, and let it vindicate the justice of the verdict: this shows that God had examined the character of every person in the world before he pronounced it universally corrupt, for there being one good man he smiled upon him.

Present God's resentment of man's wickedness not as the verdict of an unconcerned spectator but as the grief of one injured and affronted by it, who saw it as a tender father sees the folly and stubbornness of a rebellious child, which not only angers him but grieves him. Then handle the strange expressions carefully, for they are after the manner of men and must be understood so as not to reflect upon the honour of God's immutability or felicity. This language does not imply any passion or uneasiness in God, since nothing can create disturbance to the Eternal Mind; it expresses his just and holy displeasure against sin as odious to his holiness and against sinners as obnoxious to his justice. Gather the scriptural expressions of it: he is pressed by the sins of his creatures, wearied, broken, grieved, and here grieved to the heart, as men are when they are wronged and abused by those they have been very kind to, and therefore repent of their kindness and wish they had never fostered that snake in their bosom which now hisses in their face and stings them to the heart. Then turn it upon the reader at once, which is the whole use of the passage: does God thus hate sin, and shall we not hate it? has our sin grieved him to the heart, and shall we not be grieved and pricked to the heart for it? Then set Noah against the world and mark the distinction put upon him. When God was displeased with the rest of mankind he favoured Noah, and this vindicates God's justice in his displeasure against the world, showing that he had strictly examined the character of every person in it before pronouncing it universally corrupt; for, there being one good man, he found him out and smiled upon him. It also magnifies his grace, that Noah was made a vessel of mercy when all mankind besides had become the generation of wrath, and distinguishing favours bring under peculiarly strong obligations. Probably Noah did not find favour in the eyes of men, who hated and persecuted him because both by his life and his preaching he condemned the world; but he found grace in the eyes of the Lord, and that was honour and comfort enough. God made more account of Noah than of all the world besides, and this made him greater and more truly honourable than all the giants who became mighty men and men of renown. Let this be the summit of our ambition, to find grace in the eyes of the Lord.

debates.question: How can it be said that it repented the Lord?

sides.position: An anthropopathy: as a potter who has made a vessel that does not please him repents of it and breaks it in pieces
The words cannot reflect on God's immutability, since nothing can disturb the Eternal Mind; they express his just displeasure, as of a man wronged by those he had been kind to
Repentance cannot take place in God, since nothing happens to him unforeseen; the Spirit accommodates himself to our capacity
Not an accommodation but an antinomy: sovereignty and human freedom must both be true, though our mental powers are too limited to combine them

debates.question: Why does the sentence reach the animals?

sides.position: Creatures made for man's sake and living by his use were drawn into his ruin when he fell, the end of their creation being frustrated
The text says only that the destruction reaches to them, not that every animal perished; wild beasts go unmentioned, probably because the domestic cattle would suffer most
Of preventing mercy, not by his own industry or merit; the commencement of the favour was gratuitous
On the three grounds the text supplies, that he was just, perfect in his generation, and walked with God
The finding of one good man vindicates the justice of the verdict passed on all the rest

outliers.note: Alone declines to resolve the divine repentance as a figure and frames it instead as an antinomy, holding that omniscience and human freedom must both be true and that Scripture keeps the second in the foreground because responsibility depends upon it.

Alone turns the verse into an argument against the angel theory, since a race so begotten would not be the race first created by God in Adam but a grotesque product of the Adamitic factor and an entirely foreign angelic one.

themes: God saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth
it repented the LORD that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him at his heart
But Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD

9.pericope_label: The generations of Noah; the earth corrupt and filled with violence

schools.summary: Begin with the two words of the commendation, and refuse to inflate either. Just is literally righteous, one whose actions were sufficiently upright to exempt him from the punishment inflicted upon the rest of mankind — righteous, that is, in his moral relation to God. Perfect means sound, healthy, and conveys no idea of sinlessness; it answers to the Latin integer, whence our word integrity, and not to perfectus, so that what is asserted is blamelessness in character and conduct rather than a spotless nature. Then separate two Hebrew words the English blurs together, for generations at the head of the verse is toldoth and generations at its close is doroth, an entirely different word which simply means his contemporaries, the families which passed by Noah, the Nestor of his time. His righteousness and integrity were manifested in his walking with God, in which he resembled Enoch. Turn next to the term earth, and observe that this is the larger word, occurring no less than six times in three verses and thereby indicating a more widespread calamity than if adamah only had been used, as it was in the earlier sentence of destruction. Yet do not overreach: the earth that was corrupt before God was not the whole material globe, but that part which man, notably the gibborim already named, had filled with violence. Whithersoever man's violence had spread, there his home and all his works, his builded cities, his tilled land, his cattle and stores, must be entirely swept away, and an absolutely new beginning was to be made by Noah, such as Adam had to undertake when he was expelled from Paradise. Explain also why material things share the sentence when they are incapable alike of moral good or evil: man had made them the instruments of working his carnal will, and because of the associations connected with them they must be effaced, or rubbed out. On corrupt before God, note that the divine name points back to the name used of Noah's walk, and that the corruption became so conspicuous to God that He could not refrain from punishment. Last, fix the reference of all flesh here, and be strict about it. It is the whole human race which had resisted the influence of the Spirit of God and become flesh, and the term in this verse cannot include the animal world, since the expression corrupted its way is applicable to man alone. That the same term afterwards embraces both men and animals, and later still denotes the animal world only, is no objection but the very proof that its precise meaning must always be settled from the sentence in which it stands.

Take the opening formula as a hinge in the book's structure. It is the account of his posterity, of the persons that sprang from him and peopled the earth after the flood, who are named in the next verse, what follows between being read as a parenthesis; as the line was carried from Adam to Noah, so the old world ending at the flood, the genealogy of the new world begins with Noah. Note that Aben Ezra and Ben Gersome instead take the word as events, the things which the days brought forth. On the word properly meaning generation, allow that it has sometimes a more extended sense and applies to the whole history of a life, which seems to be its meaning here; and mark that the second word is different again, signifying an age, or the time of a life. Then weigh the two titles together, for the pairing is not careless. The second is opposed to what is deceitful, pretended, and vain; the world, being always influenced by external splendour, estimates justice not by the affection of the heart but by bare works, whereas if we desire to be accounted righteous before God we must not only regulate our hands and eyes and feet in obedience to his Law, but integrity of heart is above all things required and holds the chief place in the true definition of righteousness. Guard the term from a false severity: they are called just and upright not who are in every respect perfect and in whom there is no defect, but who cultivate righteousness purely and from their heart. Then press the emphatic clause, in his generations. It was a remarkable instance of constancy that Noah, being surrounded on every side with the filth of iniquity, should hence have contracted no contagion; we know how great is the force of custom, so that nothing is more difficult than to live holily among the wicked, and scarcely is there one in a hundred who has not in his mouth that diabolical proverb, we must howl when we are among the wolves. Draw the lesson without softening it: we are instructed what we ought to do though the whole world were rushing to its own destruction. Had Noah had respect to man he would have been cast into a profound labyrinth; his only remedy was to disregard men, that he might fix all his thoughts on God and make Him the sole Arbiter of his life. On the corruption itself, say that the inhabitants were corrupt both in principle and practice, in the worship of God, worshipping the creature besides the Creator, and in their manners toward one another, and that they did these things openly and impudently, without dread of his displeasure. On the looking, observe that it is spoken as if he had never looked before, whereas his eyes are always upon the earth; the word marks the special notice he took, and the added behold marks the certainty, since the omniscient God has declared it. Note too that in this last clause flesh is not used in a bad sense, but stands simply for man, as when all flesh shall see the glory of the Lord.

Lay out Noah's character in its order, and begin where the New Testament begins. He was justified before God by faith in the promised seed, for he was an heir of the righteousness which is by faith; he was sanctified, and had right principles and dispositions implanted in him; and he was righteous in his conversation, one that made conscience of rendering to all their due, to God his due and to men theirs. Then take the walking with God as the sum of the rest, done as Enoch had done it before him. But do not let the closing words drop, for the whole weight of the commendation rests on them: he did this in his generation, even in that corrupt degenerate age. It is easy to be religious when religion is in fashion, but it is an evidence of strong faith to swim against the stream and to appear for God when no one else appears for him, and this is upon record to Noah's immortal honour. Then turn to the world he stood against, and note plainly that the description here follows the Puritan exposition almost sentence for sentence, so that the substance is borrowed rather than independently observed. Corrupt before God means corrupt in the matters of God's worship: either they had other gods before him, or they worshipped him by images, or they were corrupt and wicked in despite of God. Filled with violence means injustice towards men, and the state of things is worth spelling out, since there was no order nor regular government, no man was safe in the possession of that which he had the most clear right to, and there was nothing but murders, rapes and rapines. On the looking, make the point evidential: God was himself an eye-witness of the corruption that was in it. And on the last clause, do not let it be narrowed to a district or a nation, for it was not some particular nations that were thus wicked, but the whole world so, and there was none good beside Noah. Let the hearer feel what that means before the chapter goes further: one household in an entire earth, and the promise of God resting on it.

Ask first why the wickedness of that generation is spoken of here again, when it has been described already, and give the two answers together: either as a foil to Noah's piety, since he was just and perfect when all the earth was corrupt, or as a further justification of God's resolution to destroy the world, which he was now about to communicate to his servant. Then set out the indictment in three parts. First, all kinds of sin were found among them. They were corrupt before God, that is, in the matters of God's worship — either they had other gods before him, or they worshipped him by images, or they were corrupt and wicked in despite and contempt of God, daring him and defying him to his face; and the earth was also filled with violence and injustice towards men, so that there was no order nor regular government, no man was safe in the possession of that which he had the most clear and incontestable right to, no, not the most innocent life, and there was nothing but murders, rapes, and rapine. Draw the note from it: wickedness, as it is the shame of human nature, so it is the ruin of human society; take away conscience and the fear of God, and men become beasts and devils to one another, like the fishes of the sea, where the greater devour the less; sin fills the earth with violence, and so turns the world into a wilderness. Second, the proof and evidence of it were undeniable, for God looked upon the earth and was himself an eye-witness of the corruption that was in it; the righteous Judge in all his judgments proceeds upon the infallible certainty of his own omniscience. Third, and this most aggravated the matter, the contagion had spread universally, for it was not some particular nations or cities that were thus wicked, but the whole world of mankind, and there was none that did good, no, not one besides Noah. Close with the warning that carries the whole passage over to the hearer. When wickedness has become general, universal ruin is not far off; while there is a remnant of praying people in a nation to empty the measure as it fills, judgments may be kept off a great while, but when all hands are at work to pull down the fences by sin, and none stand in the gap to make up the breach, what can be expected but an inundation of wrath? And add, as the passage turns toward Noah, that the secret of the Lord is with them that fear him.

Events, the things which the days brought forth and which befell him — so Aben Ezra and Ben Gersom
The whole history of a life, since what follows is a description of the man rather than a list

Neutral here, standing simply for mankind without censure, as when all flesh is said to see the glory of the Lord

outliers.note: Alone makes the righteousness forensic before it is practical, taking Noah as justified before God by faith in the promised seed and heir of the righteousness which is by faith, and only then righteous in his conversation.

Alone limits the scope of the destruction from the vocabulary itself, observing that though the larger word for earth occurs six times in three verses it means not the whole material globe but whithersoever man's violence had spread.

The earth also was corrupt before God, and the earth was filled with violence

13.pericope_label: The end of all flesh; make thee an ark of gopher wood

schools.summary: Two readings of the opening sentence stand side by side here, and both are worth giving. One takes it as a metaphor from the customs of earthly kings: before an order is executed the decree is presented to the sovereign, that it may finally be examined, and if approved receive the sign manual, upon which it becomes law. The other presses the idiom, since the phrase rendered come before, when applied to rumours, invariably signifies to reach the ear; on that reading the noun is not the end in the sense of destruction, but the end, that is the extremity, of a depravity which leads to destruction. Then note that the verb rendered destroy is not the one used in the earlier sentence, but the one translated had corrupted a verse before, meaning to bring to ruin, to devastate; the lex talionis is obvious, since because all flesh had destroyed its way it should be destroyed along with the earth. Render the last words even the earth rather than with the earth: I will bring them to nought, even the whole present constitution of earthly things. On the vessel, admit the difficulty honestly, for the word is so archaic that scholars neither know its derivation nor even to what language it belongs; it is probably Egyptian, is used elsewhere only of the vessel in which Moses was placed, and comes to us through the Vulgate arca. What is certain is that it was an oblong box, not capable of sailing, but intended merely to float — and observe that where the Chaldean account of the deluge speaks everywhere the language of a maritime people, this history is as plainly the work of a people living inland. Gopher is likewise a word occurring nowhere else; it is related to the word for resin and to the Greek name of the cypress, and that tall, upright evergreen of great durability, anciently much valued for shipbuilding, is most likely what is meant. Rooms is literally nests, small cells or cabins arranged in three tiers, so that the interlacing of the timbers might aid in holding the whole structure together, and the pitch is natural bitumen, which argues that the ark was built in some country where that product is easily obtainable. Reckon the cubit at eighteen inches, being the length of the arm from elbow to fingertip and a fourth of a man's height, which gives a vessel four hundred and fifty feet long, seventy-five broad, and forty-five deep, smaller than the Great Eastern but hard enough to build without her breaking her back in tempestuous weather. Last, the light. The word means brightness, and in the dual it is the ordinary term for midday; it is not the lattice of a later chapter nor the aperture of another, but a space for light, and for air as well, since a hull pitched within and without would leave the two lower storeys fit only for stores and ballast. Read the direction as an open cubit left unboarded all round beneath the overhanging eaves, the builder working upward from beneath until that last course, which is not to be finished.

Take the words God said unto Noah as themselves the proof of the favour just announced, since God spake to him, told him what he had observed and what he was determined to do, and gave him directions for the security of himself and his family. Then set the revelation out in three parts, and keep them distinct: the counsel of God respecting the destruction of the world was revealed to him; the command to build was given; and safety was promised him if, in obedience, he would take refuge in the ark. Note that the Apostle, proclaiming the faith of Noah, joins fear and obedience with confidence, and say why the warning was mercy. So long as life was promised him on earth he would never have been so intent as he ought in the building; but being alarmed by the judgment of God he earnestly embraces the promise of life given to him, no longer relying upon the natural causes or means of life, but resting exclusively on the covenant by which he was to be miraculously preserved. No labour is now troublesome or difficult to him, for the spur of God's anger pierces him too sharply to allow him to sleep in carnal delights or to faint under temptations. Draw the doctrine of faith out of it: when faith is treated of simply, mercy and the gratuitous promise come into the account, but when we wish to express all its parts, fear also must be joined with it, for no one will ever seriously resort to the mercy of God but he who, touched by God's threatenings, dreads that judgment and anxiously sighs for the remedy of his evils. On the structure, restrain curiosity: there is no reason why we should anxiously inquire, except so far as our own edification is concerned. Note that it is not called a ship, for it was not made for sailing to any distant parts, but is a chest, flat bottomed and sloping upwards, made for floating; that the Targums and the more ancient Rabbins take the wood for cedar, while others say box, pine, fir, or the plane, but the cypress bids fairest, being nearest to the Hebrew in sound and a wood very durable and incorruptible, of which Alexander made a navy in the gardens about Babylon. On the size, meet the old scoff that a third part of such a space would scarcely contain four elephants. Some answer it by Origen's geometrical cubit, six times the common one, and Augustine assents; but though Moses had been educated in all the science of the Egyptians, he everywhere spoke in a homely style to suit the capacity of the people, calling the stars two great lights according to their appearance rather than according to truth, and he is not likely to have turned geometer here. What the measure of the cubit then was, we need not know: it is enough that God, whom without controversy we acknowledge to be the chief builder of the ark, well knew what the place he described was capable of holding. If you exclude the extraordinary power of God from this history, you declare that mere fables are related. On the window, some Jewish writers make it a precious stone fetched from Pison, lighting the ark like a great chandelier; but a window it was, since Noah is afterwards said to open it.

Handle the philology first, since almost every term here is disputed. The word for ark is used only of this vessel and of that in which Moses was preserved, and signifies no more than our word vessel in its common acceptation, a hollow place capable of containing persons and goods, without any particular reference to shape or form. For the wood, set out the case for cypress in order: the Greek name of the cypress may be formed from the Hebrew, since taking away the termination leaves the two words in near resemblance; the cypress is not liable to rot nor to be injured by worms; it was anciently used for ship-building; and it abounded in Assyria, where it is probable the ark was built. Then admit the doubt, for the Septuagint renders of square timber and the Vulgate of planed timber, so that it is evident those translators knew not what wood was intended, while the Syriac and Arabic trifle with the passage and render it wicker work, as if the ark had been a great basket. Do the same with the light: the original signifies clear or bright, one ancient version gives a transparency and another the noon, and one Jewish paraphrast supposes a precious luminous stone; it is probably a word to be taken collectively, signifying apertures for air and light, and the direction about the cubit probably means that the roof was left a cubit broad at the apex and did not terminate in a sharp ridge. On the dimensions, do not settle for the short cubit. Greaves, who travelled in Greece, Palestine and Egypt to ascertain the measures of antiquity and measured the pyramids against the accounts of Herodotus and Strabo, found the cubit nearly twenty-two inches, which makes the ark five hundred and forty-seven feet long, ninety-one feet two inches broad, and fifty-four feet eight inches high, a vessel computed at eighty-one thousand and sixty-two tons burden. Then meet the objection that the capacity was too small by counting rather than by assertion: excluding the whale kind, the first class of animals yields but forty-three genera, and excluding the web-footed fowls, which could live in the water, the birds yield seventy-four, while of quadrupeds it has been shown that only seventy-two species needed a place in the ark. On the destruction, note that it reached the terrestrial animals which could not live in the waters, and that destroying the earth may probably mean the alteration of its constitution, the terrestrial substance amalgamated with the waters and its materials afterwards settling in beds or strata according to their respective gravities, though this theory is disputed by others. Where the practical use of the ark is drawn, the wording follows the Puritan exposition closely: God could have secured Noah by the ministration of angels, without putting him to any care or pains, but chose to employ him in making that which was to be the means of his preservation, both for the trial of his faith and obedience, and to teach us that we cannot work out our salvation without God, and that he will not without us.

Begin by observing how much the text itself makes of this man. God's favour to him was plainly intimated in what was said of him just before, where his name is mentioned five times in five lines when once might have served to make the sense clear, as if the Holy Ghost took a pleasure in perpetuating his memory; but it appears much more in what is now said to him, in the informations and instructions here given. God here makes Noah the man of his counsel, communicating to him his purpose to destroy this wicked world by water. As afterwards he told Abraham his resolution concerning Sodom, saying, Shall I hide from Abraham the thing that I do? so here, shall I hide from Noah the thing that I do, seeing that he shall become a great nation? Take the note that follows as the doctrine of the passage: the secret of the Lord is with those that fear him. It was with his servants the prophets by a spirit of revelation, informing them particularly of his purposes; it is with all believers by a spirit of wisdom and faith, enabling them to understand and apply the general declarations of the written word, and the warnings there given. Then take the announcement itself in the order it is delivered. God told Noah, in general, that he would destroy the world: the end of all flesh has come before me; that is, the ruin of this wicked world is decreed and determined, and it has come, that is, it will come surely, and come quickly. Ask why the warning was given to a preacher, and answer it from Noah's office: it is likely that in preaching to his neighbours he had warned them in general of the wrath of God which they would bring upon themselves by their wickedness, and now God seconds his endeavours by a particular denunciation of wrath, that Noah might try whether this would work upon them. Hence observe two things, and let them be pressed on any who speak for God to others. First, that God confirmeth the words of his messengers, so that what the faithful preacher says in general the providence of God will make good in particular. Second, that to him that has, and uses what he has for the good of others, more shall be given, and given in fuller instructions; Noah warns the world, and God answers him with the whole counsel of the deluge and the pattern of the ark. Let the hearer measure his own knowledge by that rule, and ask whether what he already knows is being spent for others or hoarded.

Eighteen inches, the length of the arm from elbow to fingertip and a fourth of a man's height, making the ark four hundred and fifty feet by seventy-five by forty-five

Make thee an ark of gopher wood
The length of the ark shall be three hundred cubits

17.pericope_label: The flood announced, the covenant established, and Noah did so

schools.summary: Mark the word for flood as another archaic term, coined expressly for the waters of Noah and used nowhere else save one psalm, where there is an evident allusion to this history; read the following words as in apposition to it, so that the sentence runs, I bring the flood, waters upon the earth, to destroy all flesh wherein is a living breath, that is, man and beast. Then face the question of extent, and do not let dogmatism settle it either way. The sentence by no means involves the theory of a universal deluge. The writer described with perfect truthfulness that of which he was either an eye-witness, or of which he had received the knowledge by tradition, or which he recorded in his own language as impressions divinely inspired in his mind by God; and we have no right to force upon him, and upon the scene so vividly described, our modern notions or our modern knowledge of the earth, with its Alps and Himalayas, its round figure, its extent and diversities, so much beyond any knowledge he could have possessed or any conception he could have formed. Add two considerations. The idea of unnecessary miracle is contrary both to the wisdom of the Almighty and to what we actually find in the Bible with respect to the exercise of supernatural power; and the narrative itself repeatedly negatives the theory that the flood extended to any great distance beyond the regions then occupied by man. It is moreover in exact accordance with the use of words in Holy Scripture that the large term, the earth, should be limited to the earth as known to Noah and his contemporaries, and the extreme antiquity of the language is itself a proof that the account was committed to writing at a time long anterior to the age of Moses. On the covenant, observe that this is a new thing in the history: there had been no covenant with Adam or with the Sethites, but in the higher state of things which began with Noah, man was to hold a more exactly defined relation to God. A necessary result of that relation was revelation, since in no other way could there be a communication between the two contracting parties; and this is why the Bible is called the Old and New Covenant, or Testament, the Greek term being of wider meaning than either word with us and signifying either an agreement between the living or the document by which a testator disposes of his property after his death. The title of covenant is the more applicable to the Scriptures of the prior dispensation, which contain a series of such relations, all preparing for the last and best and most perfect, which was a Testament ratified in the blood of Christ. Then let the closing sentence stand as it is written, with no addition: thus did Noah, according to all that God commanded him, said with regard to the building of the ark, and cited by the Apostle as faith.

Set the deluge in the memory of the nations before expounding it, for the testimony is remarkably wide. Heathen writers of all nations confirm it, only putting in Noah's place some person of great antiquity of their own: the Chaldeans Sisithrus, the Greeks and Romans Prometheus or Deucalion or Ogyges. Josephus says that all the writers of Gentile history make mention of the flood and of the ark, and produces Berosus the Chaldean, Hieronymus the Egyptian who wrote the Phoenician antiquities, Mnaseas and Nicolaus of Damascus; to whom others add Melo, who wrote against the Jews and yet speaks of a deluge at which a man with his sons escaped, and Abydenus the Assyrian, whose account agrees with the Mosaic in many things, besides what Lucian and Ovid have written, and what Plato reports of the Egyptians. Then take up the promise attached to the command, and show why it was needed. Since the construction of the ark was very difficult, and innumerable obstacles might perpetually arise to break off the work when begun, God confirms his servant by a superadded promise; for then do we freely embrace the commands of God when a promise is attached to them, which teaches us that we shall not spend our strength for nought. Answer from this the charge that the doctrine of faith leads men away from the desire of doing well: what will be the degree of our alacrity in well-doing unless faith enlighten us? The promises of God alone are they which quicken us and inspire each of our members with vigour to yield obedience; without them we not only lie torpid in indolence, but are almost lifeless, so that neither hands nor feet can do their duty. As often, therefore, as we become languid or more remiss than we ought to be in good works, let the promises of God recur to us, to correct our tardiness. State the sum of the covenant plainly, for there is an understood antithesis in it: Noah should be safe although the whole world should perish in the deluge, the whole world being rejected while the Lord established a peculiar covenant with him alone. Add what else it carried, since it looked beyond the water: that he should be preserved while building from the rage of wicked men, that he and his should come safe out and repeople an earth never again to be so destroyed, and that the promised seed should spring from him, for the fulfilment of which he and his family were spared. On the pairs, be exact: two of each sort at least were to be brought and not fewer, though of the clean there were to be seven; and since mention is made only of the propagating of offspring, the number is not pressed here but males are simply coupled with females, that Noah might perceive how the world was to be replenished. Then measure the man by the labour. The prodigious size of the ark might have overwhelmed all his senses, so as to prevent him from raising a finger to begin the work; let the reader reflect on the multitude of trees to be felled, the great labour of conveying them, the difficulty of joining them together, and that the holy man was required to be engaged more than a hundred years in this most troublesome labour, among neighbours whom his building virtually doomed, and who, unless restrained by the mighty hand of God, would have stoned him a hundred times.

Begin with the singularity of the word, for it is used only to designate the general deluge and is never applied to signify any other kind of inundation. Ask whether the Holy Spirit does not intend by this to show that no other flood was ever like this one, and that it should continue to be the sole one of the kind; there have been many partial inundations in various countries, but never more than one general deluge, and we have God's own promise that there shall never be another. Then open the word covenant from its root, which is to purify or cleanse, so that it signifies properly a purification or a purifier — because in all covenants made between God and man, sin and sinfulness were ever supposed to be on man's side, and God could not enter into any engagement with him without a purifier. Hence in all covenants a sacrifice was offered for the removal of offences, hence the same word signifies both the covenant and the sacrifice offered on the occasion, and hence Christ, the great atonement and purifier, bears that very word as his title. Describe the ancient rite, since it explains the language of the prophets: a sacrifice was provided, its throat was cut and its blood poured out before God, the whole carcass was divided from head to rump so as to make exactly two equal parts, these were placed opposite to each other, and the contracting parties passed between them, or entering at opposite ends met in the centre and there took the covenant oath. Then define the thing itself with Ainsworth, as a disposition of good things faithfully declared, which God here calls his, as arising from his grace, but which implies conditions on man's part and is therefore also called ours; the apostles term it a testament, and of both properties it may be named a testamental covenant. Apply it to this case in two clauses: on God's part, that he should save Noah and his family from death by the ark; on Noah's part, that he should in faith and obedience make and enter into it, so committing himself to God's preservation. On the animals, note the economy of the divine dealing. God might have destroyed all the animal creation and created others to occupy the new world, but he chose rather to preserve those already created; nothing should be wantonly wasted, nor power or skill lavished where no necessity exists, and yet it required more means and economy to preserve the old than to have created new ones. Close with the hundred and twenty years. He prepared the ark, and through all that time preached righteousness to that sinful generation, and did so, we are told, by the Spirit of Christ, since only through him could the doctrine of repentance ever be successfully preached. Those people are represented as shut up in prison, arrested and condemned by God's justice, but graciously allowed that space to repent in; the respite was an act of great mercy, and no doubt many who died in the interim availed themselves of it and believed to the saving of their souls, but the great majority did not, else the flood had never come.

Take Noah's care and diligence in building the ark under three heads, and let the last verse of the chapter carry all three. First, as an effect of his faith in the word of God. God had told him he would shortly drown the world; he believed it, feared the threatened deluge, and in that fear prepared the ark. Note that we ought to mix faith with the revelation God has made of his wrath against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, and that the threatenings of the word are not false alarms. Then rehearse what might have been objected against the credibility of the warning, and rehearse it fully, because every objection has a modern counterpart. Who could believe that the wise God, who made the world, should so soon unmake it again; that he who had drawn the waters off the dry land should cause them to cover it again? How would this be reconciled with the mercy of God, which is over all his works, especially that the innocent creatures should die for man's sin? Whence could water be had sufficient to deluge the world? And if it must be so, why should notice be given of it to Noah only? Noah's faith triumphed over all these corrupt reasonings. Second, as an act of obedience to the command of God. Had he consulted with flesh and blood, many objections would have been raised against it: to rear a building such a one as he never saw, so large and of such exact dimensions, would put him upon a great deal of care, and labour, and expense; it would be a work of time, for the vision was for a great while to come; his neighbours would ridicule him for his credulity, and he would be the song of the drunkards, his building being called Noah's folly; and if the worst came to the worst, each would fare as well as his neighbours. But these, and a thousand such objections, Noah by faith got over. Describe the obedience itself in its two qualities. It was ready and resolute, for thus did Noah, willingly and cheerfully, without murmuring and disputing: God says, do this, and he does it. And it was punctual and persevering, for he did all exactly according to the instructions given him, and, having begun to build, did not leave off till he had finished it. Let the application be as blunt as the text: so did he, and so must we do. Third, and last, as an instance of wisdom for himself, thus to provide for his own safety while there was yet time to provide it.

debates.question: How far did the flood reach?

sides.position: Universal: heathen writers of all nations confirm it, each putting its own ancient worthy in Noah's place, and Josephus and Eusebius collect their testimonies

The words by no means require a universal deluge; the writer described faithfully what he had seen or received, and we may not force upon him our modern knowledge of the earth, nor suppose unnecessary miracle

debates.question: What is the covenant established with Noah?

sides.position: The beginning of a new order, man holding from Noah a more exactly defined relation to God, of which revelation is the necessary result
A word rooted in the sense of purifying, so that it serves both for the covenant and for the sacrifice which ratified it, and is applied as a title to Christ
The concrete promise: kept from the rage of wicked men while he built, saved in the ark, brought out to repeople an earth never so destroyed again, and the promised seed springing from him
The covenant of providence, that the course of nature should be continued to the end of time notwithstanding the interruption the flood would give it
A promise superadded to a hard command, since we freely embrace God's commands only when a promise teaches us that we shall not spend our strength for nought

debates.question: Were the creatures taken in pairs only?

sides.position: Two of each sort at least were to be brought and not fewer, though of the clean sort there were to be seven

Not a count but a coupling: since only the propagating of offspring is in view, the number is not stated but males are joined with females, that Noah might perceive how the world was to be replenished

outliers.note: Alone treats the hundred and twenty years as a preaching commission, holding that Noah preached righteousness all that while by the Spirit of Christ to men arrested and condemned but graciously respited, and that many who died in the interim believed to the saving of their souls.

Alone makes Noah a type of Christ in his fear, faith and obedience — the builder of the church which the ark figured, its pilot through the tempestuous sea of this world, and the provider of all things for its sustenance.

themes: behold, I, even I, do bring a flood of waters upon the earth
But with thee will I establish my covenant
Thus did Noah; according to all that God commanded him, so did he
